topics.name: Richard Feynman
topics.kicker: Quantum electrodynamics pioneer · Diagrams, bongos, and the _Challenger_ probe
topics.briefing: Richard Feynman was an American physicist who loved puzzles, practical jokes, and playing the bongo drums. He shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for quantum electrodynamics, the theory of how light and electrons interact, and he invented simple sketches, now called Feynman diagrams, to keep track of what particles do when they meet. In 1986, at a televised hearing, he showed how cold had stiffened the rubber O-rings that failed on the space shuttle _Challenger_.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a 1959 talk titled “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” this physicist asked why the entire _Encyclopaedia Britannica_ could not be written on the head of a pin, an idea later credited with inspiring nanotechnology. He gave that talk at Caltech, where he taught for most of his career.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for quantum electrodynamics and drew famous diagrams of particle interactions.

tossups.p: This scientist wrote that “for a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled,” in an appendix to a report on a 1986 disaster. He wrote it as a member of the Rogers Commission, set up by President Ronald Reagan.
tossups.r: At a televised hearing, he dunked a clamped O-ring sample in ice water to show that cold made it stiff. For 10 points, name this physicist who helped investigate the _Challenger_ disaster.

tossups.p: Freeman Dyson showed that this physicist’s approach to quantum electrodynamics matched the very different methods of Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga [“TOH-moh-NAH-gah”], who had worked out the same theory on their own. This physicist’s version relied on simple pictures, while Schwinger’s relied on pages of equations.
tossups.r: All three men shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this American physicist whose namesake diagrams show particles meeting and trading other particles.

tossups.p: This physicist described an antiparticle as an ordinary particle moving backward in time. In the sketches of particle collisions that he introduced in the late 1940s, a photon passing between two electrons is drawn as a wavy line.
tossups.r: Those sketches became known as diagrams named for him. For 10 points, name this American physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize.

tossups.p: While working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, this young physicist amused himself by cracking open his colleagues’ safes and filing cabinets. Stories like that one fill a best-selling 1985 book whose title begins _Surely You’re Joking_, which he told to his drumming partner, Ralph Leighton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bongo-playing physicist who won the 1965 Nobel Prize for quantum electrodynamics.

tossups.p: Three red volumes, edited with Robert Leighton and Matthew Sands, collect the lectures this man gave to beginning physics students at Caltech in the early 1960s. Those books, published in the 1960s, grew out of recordings of his classes.
tossups.r: This man also invented diagrams for drawing particle interactions. For 10 points, name this physicist who explained the _Challenger_ shuttle’s O-ring failure.

tossups.p: This physicist gave the name “partons” to tiny, pointlike pieces inside protons that explained late-1960s experiments at the Stanford Linear Accelerator, in which fast electrons bounced off protons. Partons were later identified as quarks and gluons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Caltech physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize and invented diagrams of particle interactions.

tossups.p: This physicist’s 1942 Princeton thesis, supervised by John Wheeler, led to his “sum over histories” method, which adds up every possible path a particle could take from one point to another. He taught at Cornell before spending the rest of his career at Caltech.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for quantum electrodynamics.

tossups.p: In a 1974 commencement speech at Caltech, this scientist warned against “cargo cult science,” research that looks right on the surface but skips the honest testing that real science needs. In a 1981 talk, he suggested building computers that follow quantum rules in order to simulate nature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist known for his diagrams of particle interactions and his investigation of the _Challenger_ disaster.

tossups.p: A run of six 9s in a row that begins at the 762nd decimal place of pi is named for this physicist. His book _QED: The Strange Theory of Light and Matter_ explains, for ordinary readers, how light and electrons interact.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics and played the bongo drums.

tossups.p: This physicist wrote the memoir _What Do You Care What Other People Think?_, whose title repeats a question his first wife, Arline, used to ask him. That book also describes his work on the Rogers Commission after a 1986 space disaster.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who used a glass of ice water to show why the space shuttle _Challenger_’s O-rings failed.

tossups.p: This physicist and two other men used a technique called renormalization to get rid of the infinite answers that had ruined calculations about how electrons and light interact. The theory they rescued, nicknamed QED, makes some of the most accurate predictions in all of science.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for that theory and drew famous particle diagrams.

tossups.p: A 1981 BBC television interview with this physicist was titled _The Pleasure of Finding Things Out_, a name later given to a book of his short works. In it, he described how his father taught him that knowing the name of a bird tells you nothing about how the bird actually behaves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American physicist, a Nobel winner, who played the bongos and invented diagrams of particle interactions.

tossups.p: With his Caltech colleague Murray Gell-Mann, this physicist worked out a 1958 theory of the weak nuclear force, the force behind beta decay. As a young man, this physicist earned his bachelor’s degree at MIT and his doctorate at Princeton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who won the 1965 Nobel Prize and is known for his namesake diagrams.

tossups.p: In _The Character of Physical Law_, based on lectures he gave at Cornell, this physicist said, “I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.” Born in New York City in 1918 and raised in Queens, he became one of the most popular science teachers of his time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize and helped investigate the _Challenger_ disaster.

trap.title: Not Schwinger or Oppenheimer
trap.body: This man shared his Nobel Prize with Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga, who worked out the same theory in different ways, and Freeman Dyson showed that all three approaches agreed. He also worked at Los Alamos under J. Robert Oppenheimer, and many tossups about the Manhattan Project or quantum electrodynamics mention several of these physicists together.
trap.fix: Diagrams, bongos, safecracking, the ice-water O-ring demonstration, partons, the “sum over histories,” and the red Caltech lecture books all mean this man. The director of the Los Alamos lab was Oppenheimer; the other two QED Nobel winners were Schwinger and Tomonaga. If a question asks for “these diagrams,” the answer is the diagrams, not the man.

topics.name: Heat capacity
topics.kicker: Heat needed to warm something one degree · Why water heats up so slowly
topics.dates: Studied by Joseph Black in the 1760s
topics.briefing: Heat capacity tells how much heat it takes to warm something up by one degree. Water’s value is unusually high, which is why a pot of water takes a while to boil, beach sand gets hot long before the ocean does, and coastal towns have milder weather than places far inland. Scientists often compare substances by their specific heat, the heat capacity of just one gram, and water’s is about 4.18 joules per gram per degree Celsius.
topics.answerHtml: Heat capacity (accept specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, or thermal capacity; prompt on C; do not accept “latent heat”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The “lambda point” of helium, near 2.2 kelvins, is named for the Greek-letter shape that a graph of this quantity makes as helium turns into a superfluid. A metal’s value of this quantity jumps suddenly at the temperature where the metal becomes a superconductor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: In 1819, Pierre Louis Dulong [“doo-LONG”] and Alexis Petit [“puh-TEE”] found that many solid elements have nearly the same value of this quantity per mole of atoms, about 25 joules per kelvin. Diamond’s value is far lower than that rule predicts at room temperature.
tossups.r: Water has an unusually high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in joules per kelvin, which tells how much heat it takes to warm something up.

tossups.p: Stars and black holes have negative values of this quantity, meaning they actually get hotter as they lose energy. Unlike its “specific” version, the ordinary version of this quantity depends on how much material an object contains. A full swimming pool has a far larger value of it than a cup of water.
tossups.r: Water has an unusually high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Sea breezes blow onshore on sunny afternoons partly because land has a lower value of this quantity than the ocean, so the land warms up faster. Coastal towns have milder summers and winters than inland towns because of water’s high value of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise something’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Students can find a metal’s value of this quantity per gram by dropping a hot sample into water inside a coffee-cup calorimeter and measuring how much the water warms. The formula Q equals m c delta T uses that per-gram value, symbolized lowercase c.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which is unusually high for water and tells how much heat it takes to warm something up.

tossups.p: The food “Calorie” on nutrition labels is really a kilocalorie, and the original small calorie was chosen so that water’s value of this quantity per gram came out to exactly one. In joules, that per-gram value for water is about 4.18 per degree Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Car engines are cooled with water-based coolant because water’s high value of this quantity lets it soak up a lot of heat while warming only a little. Water’s high value of this quantity comes from the energy needed to break its hydrogen bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in joules per kelvin, that tells how much heat it takes to warm something by one degree.

tossups.p: The speed of sound in a gas depends on the ratio of this quantity measured at constant pressure to this quantity measured at constant volume, a ratio called gamma. For a gas, the constant-pressure value of this quantity is always the larger one, because some of the added heat goes into pushing the gas outward.
tossups.r: Water has a high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: On a heating curve, the slanted sections are less steep when a substance has a larger value of this quantity, while the flat sections show latent heat being absorbed during melting and boiling. Metals like copper have low values of this quantity, so they heat up quickly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which is unusually high for water and is measured in joules per kelvin.

tossups.p: Before using a calorimeter to measure a reaction, chemists find the calorimeter’s own value of this quantity, often called its “calorimeter constant.” Multiplying an object’s value of this quantity by its temperature change gives the heat it gained or lost.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: In the 1760s, the Scottish chemist Joseph Black studied this quantity, and he also discovered latent heat. Black showed that equal masses of different substances need different amounts of heat to warm by the same number of degrees.
tossups.r: Water’s per-gram value of it is about 4.18 joules per degree Celsius. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is especially high for water.

tossups.p: Nitrogen gas has a larger value of this quantity per mole than argon does, because nitrogen’s two-atom molecules can also store energy by spinning. Helium and argon, both made of single atoms, have the same value of this quantity per mole.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Thick adobe or stone walls have a large value of this quantity, so they keep desert homes cool during the hot day and warm through the cold night. Oceans store huge amounts of heat because of water’s large value of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in joules per kelvin, which explains why beach sand heats up faster than the ocean.

tossups.p: Albert Einstein’s 1907 model of a solid treated its atoms as tiny vibrating springs to explain why this quantity shrinks at very low temperatures, and Peter Debye [“duh-BYE”] improved that model in 1912. Both models used the new quantum ideas of Max Planck.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to warm an object by one degree.

tossups.p: Per gram, ice has only about half the value of this quantity that liquid water has, and steam also has about half of liquid water’s value. Builders use the term “thermal mass” for a large value of this quantity in materials like concrete and brick.
tossups.r: Its per-gram form is called “specific.” For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

clues.t: The amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree
Its “specific” version is per unit mass (per gram or kilogram); its “molar” version is per mole
Water’s value is unusually high: about 4.18 joules (1 calorie) per gram per degree Celsius
Explains why beach sand gets hot long before the ocean does
Measured in joules per kelvin; the per-mass version in joules per kilogram per kelvin (or joules per gram per degree Celsius)
Q = m c ΔT: heat equals mass times the per-gram value (lowercase c) times the temperature change
Measured with a calorimeter, like a coffee-cup calorimeter; a calorimeter’s own value is its “calorimeter constant”
Land’s lower value lets it warm faster than the sea, helping cause afternoon sea breezes and milder coastal climates
Metals like copper and iron have low values (copper’s per gram is less than a tenth of water’s), so they heat up fast
Depends on how much material there is: a swimming pool’s value is far larger than a cup of water’s
On a heating curve, a larger value makes the slanted sections less steep; the flat sections show latent heat
Water’s high value, from its hydrogen bonds, makes it a good coolant for car engines
Helium’s “lambda point,” near 2.2 K, is named for the λ shape its graph makes as helium becomes a superfluid
Dulong and Petit (1819): many solid elements have about 25 joules per kelvin per mole of atoms
Einstein’s 1907 model of vibrating atoms and Debye’s 1912 model explain why it drops toward zero for cold solids
Diamond’s value at room temperature is far below what the Dulong–Petit rule predicts
Stars and black holes have negative values: they get hotter as they lose energy
Scottish chemist Joseph Black studied it in the 1760s, showing that equal masses of different substances need different amounts of heat to warm equally; he also discovered latent heat
The constant-pressure value divided by the constant-volume value is gamma, which helps set the speed of sound in a gas
For a gas, the constant-pressure value is larger than the constant-volume value, since some heat goes into pushing the gas outward
Nitrogen gas has a larger value per mole than argon, because its two-atom molecules can also store energy by spinning; single-atom helium and argon share the same value per mole
A metal’s value jumps suddenly at the temperature where it becomes a superconductor
Per gram, ice and steam each have only about half of liquid water’s value
Builders call a large value “thermal mass”: thick adobe or stone walls keep desert homes cool by day and warm at night
The original small calorie was chosen so that water’s per-gram value is exactly 1 calorie per degree Celsius; a food Calorie is really a kilocalorie

trap.title: Not latent heat
trap.body: Heat capacity tells how much heat it takes to change an object’s temperature. Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a phase change, like melting or boiling, while the temperature does not change at all. Players also blurt out “temperature,” and some questions want only the “specific” version per gram, called specific heat, which is accepted here.
trap.fix: Warming by one degree, joules per kelvin, Q = m c ΔT, water’s 4.18, sea breezes, and calorimeters point to heat capacity or specific heat. Melting or boiling at a steady temperature, the flat parts of a heating curve, and heats of fusion or vaporization point to latent heat.
trap.line: Real answer line: Heat capacity (accept specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, or thermal capacity; prompt on C; do not accept “latent heat”)

topics.name: Second law of thermodynamics
topics.kicker: Heat flows hot to cold on its own · Entropy never falls in an isolated system
topics.briefing: The second law of thermodynamics explains why hot cocoa cools down and ice melts in a warm room, but never the other way around: heat flows on its own from hot things to cold things, unless something does work to push it back. Another way to say it is that entropy, a measure of disorder, never decreases in an isolated system. It also means no engine can turn all of its heat into useful work, so even the best engine wastes some heat.
topics.answerHtml: Second law of thermodynamics (accept 2nd law of thermodynamics; prompt on second law or thermodynamics; do not accept “entropy” or another law)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his 1959 lecture “The Two Cultures,” C. P. Snow said that being unable to describe this law was like never having read a work of Shakespeare. Arthur Eddington wrote that this law holds “the supreme position among the laws of Nature.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: A ship that ran by pulling heat out of the ocean and turning all of it into work would obey the conservation of energy but break this law. Lord Kelvin and Max Planck each gave a version of this law about engines like that one.
tossups.r: That version says no engine working in a cycle can turn heat entirely into work. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics.

tossups.p: Refrigerators and air conditioners do not break this law, because they use electrical work to pump heat out of a cold space into a warmer room. Rudolf Clausius [“KLOW-zee-us”] published a famous statement of this law in 1854.
tossups.r: That statement says heat cannot pass on its own from a colder body to a warmer one. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics.

tossups.p: Sadi Carnot [“kar-NOH”] laid groundwork for this law in his 1824 book _Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire_, which argued that a heat engine must always pass some heat on to a colder body. The most efficient possible engine runs on a cycle named for Carnot.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that no heat engine can be 100 percent efficient.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny “demon” that sorts fast and slow gas molecules between two boxes, which would seem to break this law by making one box hot and the other cold without doing any work. Physicists later showed that the demon’s need to record and erase information about the molecules would save this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: Ludwig Boltzmann [“BOHLTS-mahn”] explained this law with statistics: disordered arrangements of molecules vastly outnumber orderly ones, so a system almost always drifts toward disorder. This law gives time a one-way direction that Arthur Eddington called the “arrow of time.”
tossups.r: It explains why ice melts in a warm room. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that entropy tends to increase.

tossups.p: In Isaac Asimov’s 1956 story “The Last Question,” people keep asking ever more powerful computers whether the effects of this law on the whole universe can ever be undone. Applied to the universe, this law suggests a far-future “heat death,” with no temperature differences left to power anything.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which explains why heat flows from hot objects to cold ones.

tossups.p: Erwin Schrödinger’s [“SHROH-ding-erz”] 1944 book _What Is Life?_ explored how living things stay organized despite this law. A living cell can lower the disorder inside itself only by giving off heat that raises the disorder of its surroundings even more, so life never breaks this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: In a joke summary of the laws of thermodynamics, the first law says “you can’t win” and this law says “you can’t break even.” This law explains why a car engine must waste some of the energy in its fuel as heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which also says that heat flows on its own only from hot to cold.

tossups.p: In 1865, Rudolf Clausius [“KLOW-zee-us”] summed up thermodynamics in two rules, saying that the energy of the universe is constant and that its entropy tends toward a maximum. That same year, Clausius gave entropy its name.
tossups.r: The rule about entropy is this law. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that heat flows on its own from hot to cold.

tossups.p: When the wall between a box of gas and an empty box is removed, the gas spreads through both boxes and never squeezes itself back into one, as this law predicts. The chance of all the molecules gathering back in one box by accident is so tiny that it never happens in practice.
tossups.r: Hot cocoa cools to room temperature because of this law. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: Max Planck wrote his 1879 doctoral thesis on this law. This law sets the best possible efficiency of a heat engine at one minus the ratio of its cold temperature to its hot temperature, measured in kelvins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that entropy never decreases in an isolated system.

tossups.p: Jacob Bekenstein [“BEK-en-stine”] proposed a “generalized” version of this law that counts the entropy of black holes along with ordinary entropy. Stephen Hawking at first doubted Bekenstein, but then showed that black holes give off radiation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the total entropy of an isolated system never goes down.

tossups.p: A snowflake can grow into an orderly crystal without breaking this law, because the heat it gives off as it freezes raises the disorder of the air around it even more. Ice cubes can form in a freezer for a similar reason, since the freezer dumps even more heat into the kitchen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says heat flows on its own from hot to cold.

tossups.p: In 1851, William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, stated this law as the rule that no machine can get useful work out of an object just by cooling it below the temperature of its coldest surroundings. A perpetual-motion machine that kept running by recycling its own heat would break this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that no engine can be 100 percent efficient.

clues.t: Heat flows on its own from hot objects to cold ones, never the reverse, unless something does work to push it
The entropy (disorder) of an isolated system never decreases
No heat engine can be 100 percent efficient; some heat is always wasted
Explains why hot cocoa cools to room temperature and ice melts in a warm room, but never the reverse
Rudolf Clausius laid its foundation in 1850; his 1854 statement: heat cannot pass on its own from a colder body to a warmer one
William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), 1851: no machine can get work out of an object just by cooling it below its coldest surroundings
Kelvin–Planck statement: no engine working in a cycle can turn heat from one source completely into work
Refrigerators and air conditioners obey it by using electrical work to pump heat out of a cold space
Sadi Carnot’s 1824 _Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire_ laid its groundwork; the Carnot cycle is the most efficient possible engine
Joke summary of the laws of thermodynamics: the first says “you can’t win,” and this one says “you can’t break even”
The first law says energy is conserved; this one says which way energy naturally flows
Applied to the whole universe, it suggests a far-future “heat death” with no temperature differences left
Maxwell’s demon, an imaginary molecule-sorter, seemed to break it; the cost of recording and erasing the demon’s information saves it
C. P. Snow’s 1959 lecture “The Two Cultures”: not being able to describe it is like never having read Shakespeare
Arthur Eddington: it holds “the supreme position among the laws of Nature”; he called its one-way direction the “arrow of time”
Ludwig Boltzmann explained it with statistics: disordered arrangements vastly outnumber orderly ones
Clausius (1865), the year he named entropy: the energy of the universe is constant, and its entropy tends toward a maximum
Gas let into an empty box spreads through both boxes and never squeezes itself back into one; the odds are far too tiny
Best possible engine efficiency: one minus the cold temperature divided by the hot temperature, both in kelvins
Living things obey it by raising their surroundings’ disorder; Schrödinger’s 1944 book _What Is Life?_ explored this
Max Planck wrote his 1879 doctoral thesis on it
Jacob Bekenstein proposed a “generalized” version that also counts the entropy of black holes
In Isaac Asimov’s 1956 story “The Last Question,” people keep asking ever more powerful computers whether its effects on the universe can be undone
A ship powered only by pulling heat out of the ocean would obey the conservation of energy but break this law
A snowflake can grow into an orderly crystal because the heat it releases raises the surrounding air’s disorder even more; a freezer making ice dumps heat into the kitchen

trap.title: The law, not entropy
trap.body: Entropy is a quantity (disorder, symbolized S), and the second law of thermodynamics is the rule that entropy never decreases in an isolated system. If a question asks for “this law,” saying only “entropy” is wrong; if it asks for “this quantity,” the answer is entropy. Players also mix up which numbered law is which, and saying just “second law” earns only a prompt, since Newton and Kepler have second laws too.
trap.fix: Energy being conserved is the first law; absolute zero and perfect crystals are the third law; thermometers and thermal equilibrium are the zeroth law. Heat flowing hot to cold, engines that can’t be 100 percent efficient, Carnot, Clausius, Kelvin, and Maxwell’s demon point to the second law. Say the whole name: “second law of thermodynamics.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Second law of thermodynamics (accept 2nd law of thermodynamics; prompt on second law or thermodynamics; do not accept “entropy” or another law)

topics.name: Newton’s laws of motion
topics.kicker: Three rules of force and motion · Inertia, F = ma, and action–reaction
topics.briefing: Isaac Newton’s three laws of motion explain how forces change the way things move. The first says an object keeps doing what it is doing, staying still or moving in a straight line at a steady speed, unless a force acts on it; the second says force equals mass times acceleration; and the third says every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Newton published them in 1687 in the _Principia_, and they explain everything from seatbelts to rocket launches.
topics.answerHtml: Newton’s laws of motion (accept laws of motion; do not accept “Isaac Newton” or a single law, such as “inertia”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1920, a newspaper editorial mocked Robert Goddard by claiming that a rocket could not work in empty space with nothing to push against, a mistake about the third of these laws. The paper took that claim back in 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon.
tossups.r: Rockets fly by pushing exhaust backward. For 10 points, name these three laws published by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: In a classic puzzle, a horse wonders how it can pull a cart if the cart pulls back just as hard; the answer is that the paired forces in the third of these laws act on different objects. A book’s weight and a table’s push on it are not such a pair.
tossups.r: The second of these laws says force equals mass times acceleration. For 10 points, name these three laws stated by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: The first of these laws overturned Aristotle’s idea that a moving object naturally slows down and stops unless something keeps pushing it. Galileo had paved the way by imagining a ball rolling forever on a perfectly smooth, level surface.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws, which Isaac Newton published in 1687.

tossups.p: A skydiver falling at terminal velocity feels air resistance exactly balance her weight, so by the first of these laws she keeps falling at a steady speed. A free-body diagram shows every force acting on one object so that a student can apply these laws to it.
tossups.r: The second of them says force equals mass times acceleration. For 10 points, name these three laws stated by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: In a tug-of-war, the rope pulls just as hard on both teams, so the winners are the team that pushes harder against the ground, a lesson in the third of these laws. Walking works the same way: your foot pushes back on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws, the third of which says every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

tossups.p: Edmond Halley paid to print the book that first stated these rules, after the Royal Society said it could not afford to. These rules appear near the start of that book as three “axioms,” written in Latin.
tossups.r: That book, the _Principia_, came out in 1687. For 10 points, name these three laws by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: These laws stop giving correct answers for objects moving close to the speed of light, where Albert Einstein’s special relativity takes over, and for tiny particles like electrons, which need quantum mechanics.
tossups.r: Still, they work well enough to send spacecraft to the Moon. For 10 points, name these three laws from Isaac Newton’s _Principia_.

tossups.p: Car seatbelts exist because of the first of these laws: in a sudden stop, a passenger’s body keeps moving forward until something stops it. Headrests protect necks in rear-end crashes, when the car lurches forward but the passenger’s head tends to stay behind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws stated by Isaac Newton, the first of which is called the law of inertia.

tossups.p: The SI unit of force is defined through the second of these laws as the push that makes a one-kilogram mass speed up by one meter per second every second. Doubling the net force on a cart doubles its acceleration, while doubling its mass cuts the acceleration in half.
tossups.r: The unit of force is named for their author. For 10 points, name these three laws from the _Principia_.

tossups.p: A person standing on a bathroom scale in an elevator that is speeding up on its way upward reads heavier than normal, as the second of these laws predicts. An astronaut who throws a wrench in one direction drifts off in the other, as the third of them predicts.
tossups.r: These laws include F equals m a. For 10 points, name these three laws published by Isaac Newton in 1687.

tossups.p: These laws hold exactly only in reference frames that are not accelerating; in a spinning frame, they seem to fail unless you add made-up “fictitious” forces such as the Coriolis force.
tossups.r: The first of them is often called the law of inertia. For 10 points, name these three laws stated by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: Joseph-Louis Lagrange [“luh-GRAHNJ”] and William Rowan Hamilton later rewrote the physics built on these laws using energy instead of forces. In its general form, the second of these laws says that net force equals the rate at which momentum changes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws of Isaac Newton, which include F equals m a.

tossups.p: A cannon rolls backward when it fires, and a squid jets forward by squirting water out behind it, both examples of the third of these laws. Because of that law, the total momentum of two objects that push only on each other stays the same.
tossups.r: The third of them says every action has an equal and opposite reaction. For 10 points, name these three laws that Isaac Newton published in the _Principia_.

tossups.p: René Descartes [“day-KART”] and Galileo both argued that a moving body keeps moving unless something interferes, an idea that became the first of these laws. That law explains why dishes can stay put when a tablecloth is yanked out from under them.
tossups.r: That first law is also called the law of inertia. For 10 points, name these three laws that Isaac Newton published in 1687.

tossups.p: Combined with a law of universal gravitation, these laws let their author explain Johannes Kepler’s three rules for planetary orbits and work out the paths of comets. Edmond Halley used those ideas to predict the return of the comet now named for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws, which include the law of inertia and F equals m a.
