First: an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed, unless a net force acts on it (the law of inertia)
Second: net force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma)
Third: every action has an equal and opposite reaction, so forces come in pairs
Published in Latin in 1687 in the _Principia_
The two forces in a third-law pair act on different objects, so they never cancel each other out
Rockets, squids, and recoiling cannons move by pushing something the other way (third law)
Walking: your foot pushes back on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward (third law)
Seatbelts and headrests protect riders whose bodies keep moving, or stay behind, when a car suddenly changes speed (first law)
The SI unit of force, named for their author, is defined with the second law: it speeds up 1 kilogram by 1 meter per second every second
Doubling the net force doubles the acceleration; doubling the mass cuts it in half (second law)
The first law overturned Aristotle’s idea that moving things stop unless pushed; Galileo and Descartes paved the way
A skydiver at terminal velocity feels zero net force, so she falls at a steady speed (first law)
The general form of the second law: net force equals the rate of change of momentum; the third law makes momentum conserved
A 1920 newspaper editorial claimed Robert Goddard’s rockets couldn’t work in empty space; the paper took it back in 1969, during Apollo 11
Horse-and-cart puzzle: the cart pulls back as hard as the horse pulls forward, but the paired forces act on different objects
A book’s weight and the table’s upward push are not a third-law pair, since both act on the book
Tug-of-war: the rope pulls equally on both teams, so the winners are the team that pushes harder against the ground
Edmond Halley paid to print the _Principia_ after the Royal Society couldn’t afford it; the laws appear there as three Latin “axioms”
Free-body diagrams show every force on one object so the laws can be applied to it
They hold exactly only in non-accelerating (inertial) frames; spinning frames need fictitious forces like the Coriolis force
They break down near the speed of light (special relativity) and for tiny particles like electrons (quantum mechanics)
Joseph-Louis Lagrange and William Rowan Hamilton later rewrote this physics using energy instead of forces
A scale in an elevator speeding up on its way upward reads heavier (second law); an astronaut who throws a wrench drifts the other way (third law)
With universal gravitation, they explained Kepler’s laws of planetary orbits; Halley used them to predict his comet’s return
The first law explains why dishes can stay put when a tablecloth is yanked out from under them

trap.title: All three, not one
trap.body: These three laws come up as one answer line, but each law can also be its own answer: Newton’s first law (the law of inertia), Newton’s second law (F = ma), and Newton’s third law (action and reaction). If a question asks for “these laws” or “these three laws,” naming just one law, or just “Isaac Newton,” is wrong. Inertia, acceleration, and Newton’s law of universal gravitation are separate answer lines too.
trap.fix: Listen for the pronoun: “these laws” wants the whole set, so say “Newton’s laws of motion”; “this law” wants a single one, so give its number. If the question asks for “this scientist,” the answer is Isaac Newton.
trap.line: Real answer line: Newton’s laws of motion (accept laws of motion; do not accept “Isaac Newton” or a single law)

topics.name: Max Planck
topics.kicker: German father of quantum theory · Energy comes in tiny packets called quanta
topics.briefing: Max Planck was a careful German physicist who started the quantum revolution almost against his will. In 1900, trying to explain the colors of light that hot, glowing objects give off, he proposed that energy is released only in tiny packets, or quanta, whose size is set by a number now called Planck’s constant. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics, and a European space observatory and dozens of research institutes are named for him.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This physicist later called the key step in his most famous work “an act of desperation,” since he had given up on older physics only reluctantly. He was 42 years old when he took that step.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist whose namesake constant, h, sets the size of a quantum of energy.

tossups.p: As a young student in Munich, this physicist was warned by his teacher Philipp von Jolly that physics was nearly finished, with almost nothing important left to discover. He went on to write his 1879 doctoral thesis on the second law of thermodynamics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize for discovering quanta of energy.

tossups.p: In 1899, this scientist proposed natural units of length, time, and mass built only from basic constants of nature, such as the speed of light and the constant of gravity. The tiny length in that system is about 1.6 times ten to the minus 35 meters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who started quantum theory in 1900 and whose constant is symbolized h.

tossups.p: This physicist wrote that a new scientific truth wins not by convincing its opponents, but because its opponents eventually die and a new generation grows up familiar with it. That idea is often shortened to “science advances one funeral at a time.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering energy quanta.

tossups.p: In the 1930s, this physicist served as president of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, a group of German research institutes that was refounded under his name in 1948. That society’s institutes have produced many Nobel Prize winners.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this founder of quantum theory, whose namesake constant is about 6.63 times ten to the minus 34 joule-seconds.

tossups.p: The Rayleigh–Jeans law wrongly predicted that a glowing object should give off endless energy at short wavelengths, a failure later nicknamed the “ultraviolet catastrophe.” This physicist’s radiation law avoids that problem and gives the brightness of each color of light from a perfect black body at any temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who proposed in 1900 that energy is given off in tiny packets called quanta.

tossups.p: This physicist succeeded Gustav Kirchhoff [“KEER-kof”] as a professor of theoretical physics in Berlin, and he later solved the puzzle of “black-body” radiation, a term Kirchhoff had coined. He taught at the University of Berlin from 1889 until 1926.
tossups.r: This physicist’s constant, h, times the frequency of light gives the energy of one photon. For 10 points, name this founder of quantum theory.

tossups.p: From 2009 to 2013, a European Space Agency observatory named for this physicist mapped the cosmic microwave background in great detail, helping pin down the age of the universe at about 13.8 billion years. It was launched together with the Herschel Space Observatory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering quanta of energy.

tossups.p: Since 2019, the kilogram has been defined by fixing the exact value of a constant named for this physicist, replacing a metal cylinder kept near Paris. That platinum-iridium cylinder had served as the world’s standard kilogram since 1889.
tossups.r: Multiplying this physicist’s constant by a light wave’s frequency gives the energy of one photon. For 10 points, name this German physicist who founded quantum theory.

tossups.p: This physicist was one of the first famous scientists to support Albert Einstein’s special relativity, and in 1913 he and Walther Nernst [“NAIRNST”] traveled to Zurich to recruit Einstein to Berlin. Einstein moved there the next year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize and whose constant appears in E equals h f.

tossups.p: This physicist’s radiation formula matches Wilhelm Wien’s [“VEENZ”] earlier formula for short wavelengths, but it also works for long ones. Albert Einstein extended this physicist’s idea in 1905, saying that light itself travels in packets, to explain the photoelectric effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist whose constant, h, is about 6.63 times ten to the minus 34 joule-seconds.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this future physicist was such a talented pianist that he considered a career in music before choosing physics. He was born in the port city of Kiel in 1858 and grew up in Munich.
tossups.r: Niels Bohr’s 1913 atom used this man’s constant divided by two pi. For 10 points, name this German physicist who founded quantum theory.

tossups.p: Along with Lord Kelvin, this physicist names a statement of the second law of thermodynamics saying that no engine working in a cycle can turn heat entirely into work. He spent his early career studying entropy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who proposed in 1900 that energy is given off in tiny packets called quanta.

tossups.p: On December 14, 1900, this physicist explained the reasoning behind his formula for black-body radiation to the German Physical Society in Berlin. That formula matched careful measurements, made by experimenters in Berlin, of the light given off by hot ovens.
tossups.r: That day is often called the birthday of quantum theory. For 10 points, name this German physicist whose constant is h.

tossups.p: Lise Meitner became this physicist’s assistant at the University of Berlin in 1912, at a time when women were rarely given such jobs. His doctoral students included Max von Laue [“LOW-uh”], who later showed that crystals can diffract X-rays.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize for discovering energy quanta.

clues.t: German physicist (1858–1947) often called the father of quantum theory
In 1900, proposed that energy is given off in tiny separate packets called quanta
His constant, h (about 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds), times light’s frequency gives the energy of one photon (E = hf)
Won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering energy quanta
Explained black-body radiation, the light given off by a hot, glowing object
His radiation law avoids the “ultraviolet catastrophe” of the Rayleigh–Jeans law, which predicted endless energy at short wavelengths
Einstein extended his idea in 1905, saying light itself comes in packets, to explain the photoelectric effect
Proposed natural units of length, time, and mass (1899), built only from basic constants of nature
The European Space Agency observatory named for him (launched with Herschel) mapped the cosmic microwave background from 2009 to 2013, helping fix the universe’s age at about 13.8 billion years
Since 2019, the kilogram has been defined by fixing his constant’s exact value, replacing a metal cylinder kept near Paris
Bohr’s 1913 atom used his constant divided by 2π (h-bar) for electrons’ angular momentum
Called his quantum idea “an act of desperation,” since he gave up on older physics only reluctantly
Explained the reasoning behind his black-body formula to the German Physical Society on December 14, 1900, often called the birthday of quantum theory
His Munich teacher Philipp von Jolly warned him that physics was nearly finished
Wrote his 1879 doctoral thesis on the second law of thermodynamics and studied entropy early in his career
Shares a statement of the second law with Lord Kelvin: no engine working in a cycle can turn heat entirely into work
Wrote that a new scientific truth wins because its opponents eventually die off, often shortened to “science advances one funeral at a time”
Succeeded Gustav Kirchhoff as a theoretical physics professor in Berlin, where he taught from 1889 to 1926; Kirchhoff had coined the term “black body”
Led the Kaiser Wilhelm Society in the 1930s; it was refounded under his name in 1948
An early supporter of special relativity; in 1913 he and Walther Nernst traveled to Zurich to recruit Einstein to Berlin
A talented teenage pianist who considered a music career; born in Kiel in 1858 and raised in Munich
His radiation formula matches Wilhelm Wien’s earlier formula at short wavelengths but also works at long ones
Lise Meitner became his assistant in Berlin in 1912; his doctoral students included Max von Laue

trap.title: The man, not his constant
trap.body: Many answer lines are named for this man: Planck’s constant, the Planck length, Planck units, and Planck’s law of black-body radiation. If a question asks for “this constant” or “this law,” name the thing; if it asks for “this physicist,” say Planck. Players also mix him up with Albert Einstein, who said in 1905 that light itself comes in packets, and with Max Born, another German-speaking quantum pioneer.
trap.fix: Energy packets in 1900, black-body radiation, the 1918 Nobel Prize, an “act of desperation,” and the Kaiser Wilhelm Society point to Planck. Light quanta and the photoelectric effect in 1905 point to Einstein; the probability meaning of quantum waves points to Max Born.

topics.name: Resonance
topics.kicker: Big vibrations at a natural frequency · How a well-timed push lifts a swing
topics.dates: Studied in sound by Hermann von Helmholtz, 1860s
topics.briefing: Every swing, guitar string, wine glass, and bridge has a natural frequency at which it likes to vibrate. Push it again and again at exactly that rhythm, and the vibrations grow bigger and bigger: that’s resonance. It is why a well-timed push sends a swing soaring, why a powerful singer can shatter a wine glass with one loud note, and why engineers add dampers to keep tall buildings and bridges from swaying dangerously.
topics.answerHtml: Resonance (accept word forms like resonant or resonating; prompt on natural frequency or sympathetic vibration)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: London’s Millennium Bridge closed two days after it opened in 2000, when walkers’ footsteps fell into step with its sideways sway and made it wobble more and more. Engineers fixed that bridge by adding dampers, devices that soak up the energy of this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a system vibrates more and more strongly when it is pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: The 1940 collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, nicknamed “Galloping Gertie,” is often blamed on this effect, although engineers say the true cause was a related twisting motion called aeroelastic flutter. That bridge in Washington State twisted wildly in a steady wind just four months after it opened.
tossups.r: This effect lets a well-timed push send a playground swing higher and higher. For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system is driven at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: England’s Broughton Suspension Bridge, near Manchester, collapsed in 1831 while a column of soldiers marched across it in step. Afterward, the British Army began ordering troops to break step when crossing bridges, to avoid this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which repeated pushes at an object’s natural frequency make its vibrations grow larger and larger.

tossups.p: Daniel Kirkwood found gaps in the asteroid belt where an asteroid would circle the Sun, for example, exactly three times for every one orbit of Jupiter, a gravitational case of this effect. Saturn’s moon Mimas [“MY-mus”] helps clear the Cassini Division in Saturn’s rings in the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which also lets a singer shatter a wine glass by singing its natural pitch.

tossups.p: Hermann von Helmholtz used hollow spheres with two openings, each built to respond to a single pitch, to pick out the notes hidden inside a sound through this effect. Blowing across the top of an empty bottle makes it hum by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that lets a powerful singer shatter a wine glass by matching its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Turning a radio’s tuning dial adjusts a circuit of an inductor and a capacitor so that this effect happens at the frequency of just one station. In such a circuit, energy sloshes back and forth between the inductor and the capacitor at their natural rate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system responds strongly to pushes at its own natural frequency.

tossups.p: A system’s “Q factor” tells how sharp and long-lasting this effect is, so a high-Q tuning fork rings for a long time after it is struck. Damping, such as friction, lowers and widens the peak on a graph of this effect.
tossups.r: The letter R in MRI stands for a magnetic form of this effect. For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system vibrates strongly at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Quartz watches keep time with a tiny crystal that vibrates 32,768 times per second, the rate at which this effect makes the crystal ring most strongly when an electric circuit pushes on it. That number is two to the fifteenth power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which pushing an object at its natural frequency makes it vibrate strongly, as when a swing is pushed in rhythm.

tossups.p: The “ocean” you hear when you hold a seashell to your ear is really background noise boosted by this effect inside the shell’s hollow space. The hollow body of an acoustic guitar uses this effect to make the strings’ sound louder.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which an object vibrates strongly when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: In a classic lab, students hold a humming tuning fork over a tube of water and raise or lower the water until the sound suddenly gets loud, showing this effect in the air column. Striking one tuning fork can make an identical fork nearby start humming on its own.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system vibrates especially strongly when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: The Taipei 101 skyscraper hangs a giant steel ball near its top as a tuned mass damper, which sways against the building to fight this effect during typhoons and earthquakes. Tall buildings are designed so that their natural sway does not match the shaking they are likely to face.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a system shakes harder and harder when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: A sitar has extra strings that the player usually leaves unplucked; they ring by this effect when the played strings sound their notes. Holding down a piano’s sustain pedal and singing loudly into the piano makes its strings answer back by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which vibrations at an object’s natural frequency make it vibrate strongly.

tossups.p: The vowel sounds of human speech come from peaks called formants, which this effect creates in the throat and mouth. Changing the shape of your mouth changes which pitches this effect boosts, which is how you can tell an “ee” from an “oo.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which lets a singer break a wine glass with the right note.

tossups.p: Pluto circles the Sun twice for every three orbits of Neptune, and Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede are locked in a 1:2:4 pattern; both are orbital examples of this effect. The pattern between Pluto and Neptune keeps the two from ever coming close, even though their orbits seem to cross.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a swing goes higher when pushed in rhythm with its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Cesium atomic clocks keep time by adjusting microwaves until cesium atoms respond most strongly, at a rate of about 9.19 billion vibrations per second that has defined the second since 1967. Your ear canal boosts sounds near 3,000 hertz by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which lets a well-timed push send a child on a swing higher.

clues.t: When a system is pushed again and again at its natural frequency, its vibrations grow larger and larger
Pushing a swing in rhythm with its natural frequency sends it higher and higher
A powerful singer can shatter a wine glass by loudly singing its natural pitch
Striking one tuning fork can make an identical fork nearby start humming on its own
Soldiers break step on bridges, a rule adopted after England’s Broughton Suspension Bridge, near Manchester, collapsed under marching troops in 1831
Often blamed for the 1940 Tacoma Narrows Bridge (“Galloping Gertie”) collapse, though aeroelastic flutter was the true cause
London’s Millennium Bridge wobbled and closed two days after opening in 2000; dampers fixed it
Tuning a radio adjusts an inductor–capacitor circuit so it responds to just one station’s frequency
The R in MRI stands for a magnetic version of it in atomic nuclei
A guitar’s hollow body makes the strings louder, and a seashell’s “ocean sound” is background noise boosted inside it
Classic lab: raise or lower the water in a tube under a humming tuning fork until the air column suddenly booms
Damping, such as friction, lowers and widens its peak; tuned mass dampers fight it in skyscrapers
Daniel Kirkwood’s gaps in the asteroid belt come from orbital versions caused by Jupiter, such as three asteroid orbits per Jupiter orbit
Saturn’s moon Mimas helps clear the Cassini Division in Saturn’s rings this way
Pluto orbits twice for every three Neptune orbits, which keeps them from ever coming close; Io, Europa, and Ganymede are locked in a 1:2:4 pattern
Hermann von Helmholtz used hollow spheres, each tuned to one pitch, to pick out the notes in a sound; blowing across a bottle works the same way
The Q factor measures how sharp and long-lasting it is; a high-Q tuning fork rings a long time
Quartz watch crystals vibrate 32,768 times per second (2 to the 15th power)
Taipei 101 hangs a giant steel ball near its top as a tuned mass damper
A sitar’s extra strings, usually left unplucked, ring through it, and so do a piano’s strings when you sing into it with the sustain pedal down
Vowel sounds come from peaks called formants, made by it in the throat and mouth
Cesium atomic clocks tune microwaves until the atoms respond most strongly, about 9.19 billion times per second, the rate that has defined the second since 1967
The ear canal boosts sounds near 3,000 hertz this way

trap.title: Effect, not frequency
trap.body: Resonance is the effect; the natural (or resonant) frequency is just the special frequency at which it happens, so “natural frequency” earns only a prompt and plain “frequency” is wrong. Clues about strings, organ pipes, and tuning forks can also tempt players into “harmonics” or “standing waves,” and a siren’s changing pitch is the Doppler effect, not this.
trap.fix: Vibrations that grow from well-timed pushes, shattered wine glasses, swings, swaying bridges, dampers, and tuned radios mean resonance. The special frequency itself is the natural frequency; patterns of nodes on a string are standing waves; and a moving source’s pitch shift is the Doppler effect.
trap.line: Real answer line: Resonance (accept word forms like resonant or resonating; prompt on natural frequency or sympathetic vibration)

topics.name: X-rays
topics.kicker: Invisible high-energy rays that pass through skin · Found by Röntgen, 1895
topics.briefing: In November 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a screen glowing across his darkened lab while he ran electricity through a glass tube wrapped in black cardboard. The invisible rays causing the glow could pass through skin and paper but not bone or metal, and he named them X-rays, with the X standing for “unknown.” Doctors use X-rays to find broken bones, dentists use them to find cavities, and space telescopes use them to study black holes and exploding stars.
topics.answerHtml: X-rays (accept X-radiation or Röntgen rays; prompt on electromagnetic radiation; do not accept “gamma rays”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Hospital tubes make these rays when fast electrons slam into a metal target such as tungsten and give off “braking radiation,” or Bremsstrahlung [“BREMS-shtrah-lung”], as they slow down. In 1913, William Coolidge improved those tubes by using a heated filament to supply the electrons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rays, discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen, that doctors use to see broken bones.

tossups.p: William Henry Bragg and his son Lawrence shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics for bouncing these rays off crystals to work out where the atoms sit; Lawrence was only 25 years old. Max von Laue [“LOW-uh”] had shown in 1912 that crystals diffract these rays.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rays, which lie between ultraviolet light and gamma rays on the electromagnetic spectrum.

tossups.p: In 1913, Henry Moseley [“MOHZ-lee”] measured these rays given off by different elements and showed that the periodic table should be ordered by atomic number. His method worked because each element gives off these rays at its own set of wavelengths.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rays that pass through skin but are blocked by bone.

tossups.p: Arthur Compton won a Nobel Prize after showing in 1923 that these rays bounce off electrons like billiard balls, coming out with longer wavelengths. That result helped convince physicists that light is made of particles called photons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these high-energy rays, which Wilhelm Röntgen discovered in 1895.

tossups.p: NASA’s Chandra observatory, carried into orbit in 1999 on the first space shuttle mission commanded by a woman, Eileen Collins, studies these rays from space, since Earth’s atmosphere blocks them. Chandra’s mirrors are nearly parallel to the incoming rays, because these rays reflect only at very shallow angles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this kind of high-energy radiation that dentists use to look for cavities.

tossups.p: Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for computed tomography, or CT, which combines many images made with these rays into slices of the body.
tossups.r: On ordinary images made with these rays, bones show up white. For 10 points, name these rays, which doctors use to check for broken bones.

tossups.p: One of the first images ever made with these rays showed the hand of the discoverer’s wife, wedding ring and all. Their discoverer won the first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901.
tossups.r: He named them with an X because they were unknown. For 10 points, name these rays found by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895.

tossups.p: Before some scans with these rays, patients swallow a chalky drink of barium sulfate, which blocks the rays and makes the stomach and intestines show up clearly. Technicians cover other parts of the body with aprons containing lead, which also blocks them.
tossups.r: Bones look white on images made with these rays. For 10 points, name these rays discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen.

tossups.p: Riccardo Giacconi [“jah-KOH-nee”] won the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics for founding the astronomy of these rays, which took off when his team’s rocket found the source Scorpius X-1 in 1962. That source turned out to be a neutron star pulling gas off a companion star.
tossups.r: Hot gas around black holes and neutron stars gives off these rays. For 10 points, name this type of radiation that can pass through skin and muscle.

tossups.p: From the 1920s to the 1950s, many shoe stores used “shoe-fitting fluoroscopes,” machines that used these rays to let customers look right through new shoes to see how their feet fit. Worries about radiation ended that practice.
tossups.r: Large doses of these rays can damage DNA. For 10 points, name these rays that doctors use to look at bones.

tossups.p: Higher-energy “hard” types of these rays pass through more material than lower-energy “soft” ones. These rays have shorter wavelengths than ultraviolet light, about the size of the gaps between atoms, which is why they are useful for studying crystals.
tossups.r: Element 111, roentgenium, honors their discoverer. For 10 points, name these rays used to photograph bones.

tossups.p: Rosalind Franklin’s “Photo 51,” made by sending these rays through fibers of DNA, showed an X-shaped pattern that revealed the molecule’s helix shape. Dorothy Hodgkin used these rays to work out the structures of penicillin and vitamin B12.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rays, used in crystallography, that Wilhelm Röntgen discovered in 1895.

tossups.p: While running a glass tube wrapped in black cardboard in Würzburg [“VURTS-burg”], a physicist noticed a screen coated with barium platinocyanide glowing across the room one day in November, the first sign of these rays.
tossups.r: His paper “On a New Kind of Rays” announced them at the end of 1895. For 10 points, name these rays discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen.

tossups.p: Mammograms, which help doctors find breast cancer early, use low doses of these rays. Like gamma rays, these rays are “ionizing,” meaning they carry enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, so patients are exposed to them only when needed.
tossups.r: Dentists use them to find cavities. For 10 points, name these rays that pass through skin but not bone.

tossups.p: Thomas Edison built devices called fluoroscopes that used these rays in 1896, but he gave up the work after his assistant Clarence Dally became seriously ill from exposure to them.
tossups.r: The comic-book hero Superman has a kind of vision named for these rays. For 10 points, name these rays discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen.

clues.t: Discovered by the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895
Named with an X because Röntgen did not know what they were: X stands for “unknown”
Pass through skin and muscle but are blocked by bone and metal, so doctors use them to see broken bones; bones look white on the images
Electromagnetic waves with shorter wavelengths than ultraviolet light; gamma rays lie beyond them
Dentists use them to find cavities, and mammograms use low doses of them
Their discoverer won the first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901
One of the first images showed the hand of Röntgen’s wife, wedding ring and all
Lead aprons block them; a chalky barium sulfate drink makes the stomach and intestines show up
CT (computed tomography) scans combine many images into slices; Hounsfield and Cormack won the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
Ionizing: they carry enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, and large doses can damage DNA
Earth’s atmosphere blocks them, so telescopes that study them must be in space
Max von Laue (1912) showed that crystals diffract them; crystallography uses them to find where atoms sit
Superman has a kind of vision named for them
William Henry Bragg and his son Lawrence shared the 1915 Nobel Prize for studying crystals with them; Lawrence was 25
Henry Moseley (1913) used the ones given off by different elements to order the periodic table by atomic number
Arthur Compton (1923): they bounce off electrons like billiard balls and come out with longer wavelengths
NASA’s Chandra observatory (1999) was launched on Eileen Collins’s shuttle mission; its mirrors reflect them only at very shallow angles
Riccardo Giacconi founded their astronomy; his team’s rocket found Scorpius X-1 in 1962, and he won the 2002 Nobel Prize
Made when fast electrons slam into a metal target like tungsten and give off “braking radiation” (Bremsstrahlung)
William Coolidge’s 1913 tube used a heated filament to supply the electrons
Rosalind Franklin’s “Photo 51” revealed DNA’s helix shape; Dorothy Hodgkin used them to solve penicillin and vitamin B12
Thomas Edison built fluoroscopes using them in 1896, but quit after his assistant Clarence Dally became seriously ill from exposure
From the 1920s to the 1950s, shoe stores used shoe-fitting fluoroscopes that let customers see through new shoes to check the fit
Element 111, roentgenium, honors their discoverer
“Hard” (higher-energy) ones pass through more material than “soft” ones; their wavelengths are about the size of the gaps between atoms
Röntgen saw a barium platinocyanide screen glow in Würzburg and announced the rays in “On a New Kind of Rays” (end of 1895)

trap.title: Not gamma or cathode rays
trap.body: X-rays and gamma rays are both invisible, high-energy light that can pass through matter, and their energies overlap. Gamma rays usually come from atomic nuclei, as in radioactive decay, while X-rays usually come from electrons, like those slamming into a metal target in a hospital tube. Cathode rays, which Röntgen was studying when he found X-rays, are streams of electrons, not light at all.
trap.fix: Broken bones, dentists, Röntgen, crystals, the Braggs, Moseley, CT scans, and the Chandra telescope point to X-rays. Radioactive nuclei and Paul Villard (who found them in 1900) point to gamma rays, and a beam of electrons inside a glass tube is cathode rays.
trap.line: Real answer line: X-rays (accept X-radiation or Röntgen rays; prompt on electromagnetic radiation; do not accept “gamma rays”)

topics.name: Electric current
topics.kicker: The flow of electric charge · Measured in amperes
topics.dates: First steady flow from Volta’s battery, 1800
topics.briefing: Electric current is a flow of electric charge, usually electrons drifting through a wire, and it is measured in amperes, or amps. Alessandro Volta’s battery made the first steady current in 1800, and in 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a wire carrying current made a compass needle swing. Wall outlets supply alternating current, which flips direction many times each second, while batteries supply direct current, which flows one way.
topics.answerHtml: electric current (accept current; prompt on I or flow of electrons; do not accept “voltage” or “electric charge”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Before 2019, the SI base unit of this quantity was defined by the force between two long, parallel wires placed one meter apart. Since 2019, that unit has been defined by fixing the exact value of the elementary charge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flow of electric charge, symbolized I and measured in amperes.

tossups.p: This quantity’s usual symbol, I, comes from the French phrase intensité du courant [“an-tahn-see-TAY doo koo-RAHN”]. In 1820, a French physicist showed that two parallel wires carrying this quantity in the same direction attract each other, and its SI unit is named for him.
tossups.r: It is measured with an ammeter. For 10 points, name this flow of charge, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: The Biot–Savart [“bee-OH suh-VAR”] law adds up the magnetic field made by each tiny piece of a wire carrying this quantity. In 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a compass needle swung whenever this quantity flowed through a nearby wire.
tossups.r: This quantity is symbolized I. For 10 points, name this flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: In a copper wire, the electrons that carry this quantity usually drift along at less than a millimeter per second. Because of a naming choice by Benjamin Franklin, the conventional direction of this quantity runs from positive to negative, opposite to the way the electrons move.
tossups.r: An ammeter measures it. For 10 points, name this flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: A galvanometer, named for the Italian scientist Luigi Galvani, detects small amounts of this quantity by how far its needle turns. Alessandro Volta’s pile of zinc and copper disks, announced in 1800, was the first battery to produce a steady flow of this quantity.
tossups.r: Batteries supply its direct form. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured with an ammeter in amperes.

tossups.p: Gustav Kirchhoff’s junction rule says that the total amount of this quantity flowing into any point in a circuit equals the total flowing out, because charge is conserved. In a parallel circuit, this quantity splits among the branches.
tossups.r: In a series circuit, it is the same at every point. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: In the late 1880s, Thomas Edison promoted one form of this quantity, while Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse promoted a form that reverses direction many times each second. The reversing form won out partly because transformers can raise and lower its voltage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which comes in AC and DC forms and is measured in amperes.

tossups.p: Outlets in the United States supply the alternating form of this quantity at 60 hertz, while much of Europe uses 50 hertz. Power companies send electricity over long lines at very high voltages so that less of this quantity flows, which cuts the energy wasted as heat.
tossups.r: Batteries supply its direct form. For 10 points, name this flow of charge, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: James Prescott Joule found that the heat given off by a wire each second equals the square of this quantity times the wire’s resistance. Fuses melt and circuit breakers trip when too much of this quantity flows through a circuit.
tossups.r: Ohm’s law says it equals voltage divided by resistance. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: In the Hall effect, a magnetic field pushes the moving charges that carry this quantity toward one edge of a metal strip, creating a small voltage across the strip. A ring of superconducting wire can keep this quantity circulating for years with no battery attached.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flow of charge, measured with an ammeter in amperes.

tossups.p: Michael Faraday found that the amount of metal plated out during electrolysis is proportional to this quantity multiplied by the time it flows. A good meter for measuring this quantity has almost no resistance and is connected in series with the part being tested.
tossups.r: That meter is an ammeter. For 10 points, name this flow of charge, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: About 6.24 billion billion electrons must pass a point each second to make one unit of this quantity. A lightning bolt carries tens of thousands of those units, though only for a tiny fraction of a second.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the rate at which electric charge flows, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: This quantity’s unit is the only electrical unit among the seven SI base units, which also include the meter, the kilogram, the second, and the kelvin. One of those units equals one coulomb of charge passing a point each second.
tossups.r: It is measured with an ammeter. For 10 points, name this flow of charge, measured in amperes.

tossups.p: Inside a long coil called a solenoid, the magnetic field equals the permeability of free space times the number of turns per meter times this quantity. An electromagnet gets stronger with more turns of wire or more of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flow of charge, symbolized I and measured in amperes.

tossups.p: Multiplying this quantity by voltage gives electric power in watts, so a 60-watt bulb on a 120-volt line draws half a unit of this quantity. A diode lets this quantity pass in only one direction.
tossups.r: It is symbolized I. For 10 points, name this flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.

clues.t: The flow of electric charge, usually electrons moving through a wire
Measured in amperes (amps): one ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second
Comes in alternating (AC) and direct (DC) forms; wall outlets supply AC and batteries supply DC
Symbolized I; Ohm’s law says it equals voltage divided by resistance (I = V/R)
Measured with an ammeter, which is connected in series with the part being tested
The same at every point in a series circuit; splits among the branches of a parallel circuit
Kirchhoff’s junction rule: the total flowing into any point equals the total flowing out, because charge is conserved
Hans Christian Ørsted (1820) saw it swing a nearby compass needle, showing that electricity and magnetism are connected
Its conventional direction runs from positive to negative, opposite to the electrons, because of a naming choice by Benjamin Franklin
Alessandro Volta’s pile (1800) was the first battery to give a steady flow of it
Late 1880s: Thomas Edison backed DC, while Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse backed AC; AC won partly because transformers can change its voltage
Fuses melt and circuit breakers trip when too much of it flows
Joule heating: heat given off each second equals its square times the resistance, so power lines use high voltage to keep it small
Electric power equals it times voltage (P = IV), so a 60-watt bulb on a 120-volt line draws half an ampere
A diode lets it pass in only one direction
Its symbol, I, comes from the French phrase intensité du courant
In 1820, André-Marie Ampère showed that parallel wires carrying it in the same direction attract; its unit is named for him
Before 2019, its unit was defined by the force between two parallel wires one meter apart; since 2019, by fixing the elementary charge
Its unit is the only electrical unit among the seven SI base units
Electrons carrying it through a copper wire drift at less than a millimeter per second
One ampere is about 6.24 billion billion electrons passing a point each second
A lightning bolt carries tens of thousands of amperes for a tiny fraction of a second
A galvanometer, named for Luigi Galvani, detects small amounts of it by how far a needle turns
The Biot–Savart law adds up the magnetic field made by each tiny piece of a wire carrying it
Hall effect: a magnetic field pushes its moving charges to one edge of a strip, making a small voltage across the strip
A ring of superconducting wire can keep it circulating for years with no battery attached
Michael Faraday: the metal plated out in electrolysis is proportional to it multiplied by the time it flows
A good ammeter has almost no resistance, so it barely changes what it measures
U.S. outlets supply the alternating form at 60 hertz; much of Europe uses 50 hertz
Inside a long solenoid, the magnetic field equals the permeability of free space × turns per meter × this quantity

trap.title: Current, voltage, or charge?
trap.body: Circuit tossups mix three related answers. Current is how fast charge flows (amperes), voltage is the push that drives it (volts), and charge is the stuff that flows (coulombs). Some tossups want one specific kind instead: questions about Edison, Tesla, and the “War of the Currents” often ask for alternating current, and Earth science tossups ask about ocean currents.
trap.fix: Amperes, ammeters, the symbol I, I = V/R, and Kirchhoff’s junction rule mean current. Volts and potential difference mean voltage; coulombs, Millikan’s oil drops, and “positive or negative” mean charge. If the giveaway asks for the form that reverses direction many times a second, say “alternating current.”
trap.line: Real answer line: electric current (accept current; prompt on I or flow of electrons; do not accept “voltage” or “electric charge”)

topics.name: Electric charge
topics.kicker: Positive or negative property of matter · Measured in coulombs
topics.dates: Two kinds named positive and negative by Franklin, 1740s
topics.briefing: Electric charge is a basic property of matter that comes in two kinds, positive and negative, names chosen by Benjamin Franklin. Like charges repel and opposite charges attract, which is why a balloon rubbed on your hair can stick to a wall. Charge is measured in coulombs, and every proton and electron carries the same tiny amount, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs: positive for the proton, negative for the electron.
topics.answerHtml: electric charge (accept charge; prompt on q; do not accept “electric current” or “elementary charge”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1733, Charles du Fay [“dew FAY”] described two kinds of this property, calling one “vitreous” because it came from rubbed glass and the other “resinous” because it came from rubbed amber and other resins. Benjamin Franklin later gave those two kinds new names.
tossups.r: Like kinds repel and opposite kinds attract. For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs, that comes in positive and negative forms.

tossups.p: Quarks carry fractions of this property, such as plus two-thirds or minus one-third of a proton’s amount, but they are never found alone. In a neutral atom, the positive amount of this property on the protons exactly balances the negative amount on the electrons.
tossups.r: Opposite kinds of it attract. For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs.

tossups.p: The Faraday constant, about 96,485 coulombs per mole, is the total amount of this property carried by a mole of electrons. Gauss’s law says the electric flux through any closed surface equals the amount of this property inside, divided by the permittivity of free space.
tossups.r: It is measured in coulombs. For 10 points, name this property of matter that comes in positive and negative kinds.

tossups.p: In 1785, Charles-Augustin de Coulomb [“KOO-lohm”] used a torsion balance to show that the force between two small objects carrying this property falls off with the square of the distance between them. That force is proportional to the product of the two amounts of this property.
tossups.r: Its SI unit is named for Coulomb. For 10 points, name this property, which can be positive or negative.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin pictured electricity as a single fluid, calling an object with too much of that fluid positive and an object with too little negative. In an isolated system, the total amount of this property never changes, because it is conserved.
tossups.r: Objects with the same kind of it repel each other. For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs.

tossups.p: Thales [“THAY-leez”] of Miletus is said to have noticed that amber rubbed with fur attracts bits of straw, and William Gilbert later named “electric” effects after the Greek word for amber. Amber rubbed that way picks up a negative amount of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of matter, measured in coulombs, that comes in positive and negative kinds.

tossups.p: Bringing a rubbed plastic rod near a metal sphere, without touching it, pulls the opposite kind of this property toward the near side, a process called induction. In a gold-leaf electroscope, two thin strips of gold spread apart when they carry the same kind of this property.
tossups.r: It is measured in coulombs. For 10 points, name this property that protons and electrons carry in equal and opposite amounts.

tossups.p: Robert Millikan won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics partly for measuring the smallest free amount of this property, about 1.6 times ten to the negative nineteenth coulombs. He found it by balancing tiny oil drops in an electric field between two metal plates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that protons carry in a positive form and electrons in a negative form.

tossups.p: This property is quantized, meaning that every free particle or object carries a whole-number multiple of the amount on one proton. An atom becomes an ion when it gains or loses electrons and ends up with a net amount of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs, which comes in positive and negative kinds.

tossups.p: Electric current is the rate at which this property flows, so one ampere means one unit of it passing a point each second. Lightning strikes when huge amounts of this property built up in a storm cloud jump to the ground or to another cloud.
tossups.r: Like kinds of it repel. For 10 points, name this property of matter, measured in coulombs.

tossups.p: Any extra amount of this property placed on a metal object spreads out over the object’s outer surface. A Van de Graaff [“van duh GRAHF”] generator piles up so much of this property on its metal dome that it can make a person’s hair stand on end.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs, that makes objects with the same kind repel.

tossups.p: The triboelectric [“TRY-boh-ih-LEK-trik”] series ranks materials by whether they tend to gain or lose electrons when rubbed together, which decides what kind of this property each one ends up with. Rubbing a balloon on your hair builds up a static amount of this property on the balloon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs, that can be positive or negative.

tossups.p: In 1897, J. J. Thomson measured the ratio of this property to mass for the particles in cathode rays, which turned out to be electrons. In 1932, James Chadwick discovered a particle in the nucleus that has none of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which is positive for protons and negative for electrons.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin’s famous 1752 kite experiment is said to have drawn this property from a storm cloud down a wet string to a metal key, where Franklin stored it in a Leyden jar. Franklin also gave the names “positive” and “negative” to the two kinds of this property.
tossups.r: Its SI unit is the coulomb. For 10 points, name this property, whose opposite kinds attract each other.

tossups.p: A capacitor’s capacitance equals the amount of this property stored on one plate divided by the voltage across the plates. An electric field is defined as the force on a small test object divided by the amount of this property it carries.
tossups.r: Protons carry a positive amount of it. For 10 points, name this property, symbolized q and measured in coulombs.

Electric current is its rate of flow: one ampere is one coulomb passing a point each second
An atom that gains or loses electrons ends up with a net amount and is called an ion
In a neutral atom, the protons’ positive amount exactly balances the electrons’ negative amount
A gold-leaf electroscope detects it: the two thin gold leaves spread apart when they carry the same kind

Franklin pictured electricity as a single fluid: too much made an object positive, and too little made it negative

A Van de Graaff generator piles up so much on its metal dome that it can make a person’s hair stand on end

J. J. Thomson (1897) measured its ratio to mass for the particles in cathode rays, which turned out to be electrons

A capacitor’s capacitance equals the amount stored on one plate divided by the voltage across the plates (C = Q/V)

trap.title: Charge, not current
trap.body: Electric charge is the stuff itself, measured in coulombs; electric current is how fast it flows, measured in amperes; and voltage is the push that moves it. Tossups about Millikan’s oil drops can also tempt you to say “electrons” or “elementary charge,” but when the giveaway asks for the property that comes in positive and negative kinds, the answer is just charge.
trap.fix: Coulombs, q, “positive and negative,” “like kinds repel,” conservation, and quantization mean charge. Amperes, ammeters, and I mean current; volts mean voltage. The elementary charge (about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs) is one specific amount of it, not the property itself.
trap.line: Real answer line: electric charge (accept charge; prompt on q; do not accept “electric current” or “elementary charge”)

topics.name: Hooke’s law
topics.kicker: A spring’s stretch grows with the force · F = −kx
topics.briefing: Hooke’s law says that the force needed to stretch or squeeze a spring is proportional to how far you stretch or squeeze it: pull twice as hard and it stretches twice as far. Robert Hooke first hid the idea in a scrambled Latin anagram in 1676, then revealed it two years later as “ut tensio, sic vis,” meaning “as the extension, so the force.” The rule works only up to a spring’s elastic limit.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This law was first published in 1676 as the scrambled Latin anagram “ceiiinosssttuv.” Two years later, its discoverer revealed the answer: “ut tensio, sic vis” [“oot TEN-see-oh, sik VEES”], meaning “as the extension, so the force.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the force on a spring is proportional to how far it is stretched.

tossups.p: Isaac Newton’s line about “standing on the shoulders of giants” appeared in a letter to this law’s namesake, who later claimed that Newton had taken his idea that gravity follows an inverse-square law. This law can be written with a spring constant measured in newtons per meter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, written F equals negative k x, that describes how springs stretch.

tossups.p: For solid materials, this law says that stress is proportional to strain, and the constant that links them is named for Thomas Young. Beyond a point called the elastic limit, a material stops obeying this law and is permanently stretched out of shape.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law about springs, written F equals negative k x, where k is the spring constant.

tossups.p: Chemists predict where a chemical bond will absorb infrared light by treating the bond as a spring that obeys this law, so stiffer bonds vibrate at higher frequencies. A mass hanging from a spring that obeys this law bobs up and down in simple harmonic motion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that a spring’s restoring force is proportional to its stretch.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake was the Royal Society’s first Curator of Experiments and helped survey London after the Great Fire of 1666. In his 1665 book _Micrographia_, he coined the word “cell” after looking at thin slices of cork through a microscope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, written F equals negative k x, that describes springs.

tossups.p: On a graph of force against stretch, this law appears as a straight line through the origin, and the slope of that line is the spring constant. The minus sign in this law shows that a spring pulls back opposite to its stretch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, written F equals negative k x, that describes springs.

tossups.p: Because the force in this law grows steadily with the stretch, a spring stretched a distance x stores elastic potential energy equal to one-half k x squared. So stretching such a spring twice as far stores four times as much energy.
tossups.r: Spring scales work because of it. For 10 points, name this law, written F equals negative k x.

tossups.p: According to this law, two identical springs hung side by side act like one spring that is twice as stiff, while the same two springs joined end to end are only half as stiff. A larger spring constant in this law means a stiffer spring.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the force needed to stretch a spring is proportional to the stretch.

tossups.p: Any system whose restoring force obeys this law is called a harmonic oscillator, because it vibrates in simple harmonic motion. A real spring obeys this law only until it reaches its elastic limit, past which it stays permanently stretched.
tossups.r: Spring scales use it to measure weight. For 10 points, name this law, written F equals negative k x.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake quarreled with Christiaan Huygens [“HOY-gunz”] over who first invented the balance spring, the tiny coiled spring that keeps time in a watch. In this law, a stiffer spring has a larger spring constant, measured in newtons per meter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the force on a spring is proportional to its stretch.

tossups.p: For a mass on a spring that obeys this law, the period of each bounce equals two pi times the square root of the mass divided by the spring constant, so a heavier mass bobs more slowly.
tossups.r: That bouncing is called simple harmonic motion. For 10 points, name this law, written F equals negative k x.

tossups.p: A twisting version of this law, in which the twist of a thin wire is proportional to the turning force on it, made possible the torsion balances of Charles-Augustin de Coulomb [“KOO-lohm”] and Henry Cavendish. Its minus sign shows that the force points back toward the resting position.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the force on a spring is proportional to how far it is stretched.

tossups.p: This law was explained in its discoverer’s 1678 lecture _De Potentia Restitutiva_ [“day poh-TEN-tee-ah res-tih-too-TEE-vah”], or _Of Spring_, which revealed the meaning of an anagram he had published two years earlier. That anagram’s Latin solution means “as the extension, so the force.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that a spring’s stretch is proportional to the force on it.

tossups.p: Under this law, a spring with a constant of 200 newtons per meter stretches 10 centimeters when pulled with a force of 20 newtons. A graph of force against stretch for that spring is a straight line with a slope of 200 newtons per meter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating a spring’s stretch to the force on it, written F equals negative k x.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake also gives his name to a universal joint that lets a rotating shaft drive another shaft set at an angle, as in a car’s driveshaft. Earlier, he worked as Robert Boyle’s assistant and built the air pump that Boyle used to study gases.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, written F equals negative k x, that describes springs.

clues.t: The force needed to stretch or compress a spring is proportional to how far it is stretched or compressed
Written F = −kx, where k is the spring constant and x is the stretch
Explains spring scales (force meters), which measure weight by how far a spring stretches
Doubling the force on a spring doubles its stretch
Works only up to the elastic limit; stretched past it, a spring is permanently bent out of shape
The spring constant is measured in newtons per meter; a stiffer spring has a larger one
A graph of force against stretch is a straight line through the origin, with the spring constant as its slope
The minus sign shows that the restoring force points back toward the resting position, opposite to the stretch
A stretched spring stores elastic potential energy equal to one-half k x squared
A mass on such a spring moves in simple harmonic motion; its period is 2π times the square root of m divided by k
Its namesake coined the word “cell” after viewing slices of cork in his book _Micrographia_ (1665)
First published in 1676 as the Latin anagram “ceiiinosssttuv”
Solved in 1678 as “ut tensio, sic vis”: “as the extension, so the force”
Explained in the 1678 lecture _De Potentia Restitutiva_, or _Of Spring_
For solid materials it says stress is proportional to strain; the constant linking them is Young’s modulus
Treating chemical bonds as springs that obey it predicts where they absorb infrared light; stiffer bonds vibrate faster
Two identical springs side by side are twice as stiff as one; joined end to end, they are half as stiff
Any system whose restoring force obeys it is called a harmonic oscillator
A twisting version, with the twist of a thin wire proportional to the turning force, made the torsion balances of Coulomb and Cavendish work
Isaac Newton’s line about “standing on the shoulders of giants” appeared in a letter to its namesake
Its namesake claimed that Newton had taken his idea that gravity follows an inverse-square law
Its namesake was the Royal Society’s first Curator of Experiments
Its namesake helped survey London after the Great Fire of 1666
Its namesake quarreled with Christiaan Huygens over who first invented the balance spring for watches
Its namesake worked as Robert Boyle’s assistant and built the air pump Boyle used to study gases
Its namesake’s name is also on a universal joint used in car driveshafts

trap.title: Law, constant, or motion?
trap.body: Spring tossups have several look-alike answers. This law is the rule F = −kx; the spring constant k is just one number in it, simple harmonic motion is the bouncing that results, and Young’s modulus is the stiffness constant in its version for solid materials. Clues about Robert Boyle’s air pump can also lure a wrong buzz of “Boyle’s law,” since this law’s namesake built that pump, and answering just “Hooke” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Proportional stretch, F = −kx, the 1676 anagram, and “ut tensio, sic vis” mean this law. If the giveaway asks for “this quantity” measured in newtons per meter, say spring constant; for the back-and-forth motion, say simple harmonic motion; for the pressure and volume of a gas, say Boyle’s law.
trap.line: Real answer line: Hooke’s law (prompt on Hooke or elasticity)

topics.name: Theory of relativity
topics.kicker: Einstein’s theories of space and time · Special (1905), general (1915)
topics.briefing: Albert Einstein’s theory of relativity comes in two parts. Special relativity (1905) says the speed of light is the same for everyone, so moving clocks tick slower and moving objects shrink, and it gave us E = mc². General relativity (1915) explains gravity as the bending of space and time by mass, which is why starlight curves around the Sun and why GPS satellites must correct their clocks.
topics.answerHtml: relativity (accept theory of relativity, special relativity, or general relativity; prompt on Einstein’s theory)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This theory first appeared in a 1905 paper titled “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,” written by a patent clerk in Bern, Switzerland. That paper started from two ideas: the laws of physics are the same for all steadily moving observers, and the speed of light is the same for everyone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory by Albert Einstein, which comes in special and general versions.

tossups.p: Hermann Minkowski [“min-KOFF-skee”], who had once taught math to this theory’s creator, recast part of it in 1908 using a four-dimensional “spacetime.” John Wheeler summed up another part of it by saying that spacetime tells matter how to move, and matter tells spacetime how to curve.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these theories of Albert Einstein, which come in special and general forms.

tossups.p: Muons created by cosmic rays high in the atmosphere should break apart before reaching the ground, but many survive because, according to this theory, their clocks tick slowly as seen from Earth. This theory also says that a fast-moving spaceship would be measured as shorter along its direction of travel.
tossups.r: Those effects are called time dilation and length contraction. For 10 points, name this theory of Albert Einstein.

tossups.p: In 1971, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew atomic clocks around the world on passenger jets and found that the clocks had drifted from clocks left on the ground by the amounts this theory predicts. Clocks on GPS satellites run fast by about 38 microseconds a day, so engineers correct them using this theory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory by Albert Einstein, whose special and general forms describe space and time.

tossups.p: Karl Schwarzschild [“SHVARTS-shilt”] published the first exact solution to the equations of one version of this theory in 1916, while serving in the German army during World War I. That solution describes what is now called a black hole.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory, whose general version describes gravity as curved spacetime.

tossups.p: Arthur Eddington led a 1919 expedition to photograph stars during a solar eclipse, and his measurements of starlight bending around the Sun supported this theory. This theory also explained a small, puzzling drift in Mercury’s orbit called precession.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory by Albert Einstein, whose general form treats gravity as the curving of spacetime.

tossups.p: The Pound–Rebka experiment at Harvard showed that gamma rays change frequency slightly as they travel up or down a tower, an effect of gravity predicted by this theory. Gravity Probe B confirmed that Earth’s rotation drags spacetime around with it, another prediction of this theory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory, developed by Albert Einstein in special and general versions.

tossups.p: This theory’s creator called the idea behind one version of it his “happiest thought”: a person falling freely from a roof would not feel his own weight. That idea, the equivalence principle, says that the effects of gravity and of acceleration cannot be told apart.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory by Albert Einstein, whose general form describes gravity as curved spacetime.

tossups.p: Before this theory, George FitzGerald and Hendrik Lorentz each suggested that moving objects shrink along their direction of motion, to explain why the 1887 Michelson–Morley experiment found no sign of the “aether.” This theory showed that no aether was needed at all.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory, which Albert Einstein first published in its special form in 1905.

tossups.p: In this theory’s twin paradox, a twin who rockets to a distant star and back near the speed of light comes home younger than the twin who stayed on Earth. This theory also says that nothing with mass can travel as fast as light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory of Albert Einstein, which gave the world the equation E equals m c squared.

tossups.p: In one thought experiment for this theory, lightning strikes both ends of a moving train, and a passenger and a person standing beside the tracks disagree about whether the two strikes happened at the same time. This theory showed that measurements of time and length depend on the observer’s motion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory of Albert Einstein, which comes in special and general versions.

tossups.p: In 2015, the LIGO [“LY-go”] detectors in Louisiana and Washington State recorded gravitational waves from two colliding black holes, about a century after this theory predicted such waves. Rings and arcs of light appear when a galaxy cluster’s gravity bends light from objects behind it, an effect this theory explains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory whose general form describes gravity as the curving of spacetime.

tossups.p: To keep the universe from expanding or shrinking, this theory’s creator added a cosmological constant to its equations, a move he reportedly later called his “biggest blunder.” Edwin Hubble’s 1929 evidence that the universe is expanding made that term seem unnecessary.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory by Albert Einstein, which comes in special and general forms.

tossups.p: This theory’s creator won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining the photoelectric effect rather than for this theory. The first part of this theory was published in 1905, the same year he explained Brownian motion.
tossups.r: This theory shows that mass can be turned into energy, as in E equals m c squared. For 10 points, name this theory.

tossups.p: Calculations in one version of this theory use the Lorentz factor, which grows without limit as an object’s speed approaches the speed of light. As a teenager, this theory’s creator imagined what it would be like to chase a beam of light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory, whose special form predicts that moving clocks tick slowly.

clues.t: Developed by Albert Einstein in two parts: a special theory (1905) and a general theory (1915)
Its special theory gave the equation E = mc²: mass and energy are equivalent
Its general theory describes gravity as the curving of spacetime by mass and energy
Moving clocks run slow (time dilation), and moving objects shrink along their direction of motion (length contraction)
Its special theory says the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for every observer, and nothing with mass can reach it
The twin paradox: a twin who rockets away near light speed comes home younger than the twin who stayed on Earth
Arthur Eddington’s 1919 solar eclipse expedition measured starlight bending around the Sun, supporting the general theory
The general theory explained a small, puzzling drift in Mercury’s orbit called precession
GPS satellite clocks run fast by about 38 microseconds a day and must be corrected using it
Its special theory was published in 1905, while its creator was a patent clerk in Bern, Switzerland
The 1887 Michelson–Morley experiment found no sign of the “aether”; the special theory showed that none was needed
The general theory predicts black holes and gravitational waves; LIGO first directly detected the waves in 2015
Its creator’s 1921 Nobel Prize was for the photoelectric effect, not for this theory
The general theory explains how gravity bends light from distant objects into rings and arcs, called gravitational lensing
The special theory first appeared in the 1905 paper “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies”
The special theory rests on two postulates: physics works the same for all steadily moving observers, and light’s speed is the same for everyone
Hermann Minkowski, who had once taught its creator math, recast the special theory in four-dimensional spacetime in 1908
John Wheeler’s summary of the general theory: spacetime tells matter how to move, and matter tells spacetime how to curve
Muons made by cosmic rays high in the atmosphere reach the ground only because their clocks run slow
The Hafele–Keating experiment (1971) flew atomic clocks around the world on passenger jets to test its predictions
Karl Schwarzschild published the first exact solution of its equations in 1916, while serving in World War I; it describes a black hole
The Pound–Rebka experiment at Harvard showed gamma rays changing frequency as they traveled up or down a tower
Gravity Probe B confirmed that Earth’s rotation drags spacetime around with it
Its creator’s “happiest thought”: a person falling freely would not feel his own weight, the root of the equivalence principle
George FitzGerald and Hendrik Lorentz had proposed that moving objects shrink, to explain the Michelson–Morley result
Thought experiment: lightning strikes both ends of a moving train, and two observers disagree about whether the strikes happened at the same time
Its creator added a cosmological constant to keep the universe from expanding or shrinking, reportedly later calling it his “biggest blunder”
The Lorentz factor, used in its calculations, grows without limit as an object’s speed approaches the speed of light

trap.title: Special, general, or Einstein?
trap.body: This topic asks for the theory as a whole, so “special relativity” and “general relativity” are both accepted here, the way real answer lines accept them when a question wants the overall theory. Many real tossups are about only one of the two, though, and then plain “relativity” may earn only a prompt. If every clue is about a life (birthplace, prizes, moving to Princeton), the answer is “Albert Einstein,” not his theory.
trap.fix: 1905, moving clocks, shrinking lengths, the twin paradox, muons, and E = mc² mean special relativity. 1915, curved spacetime, the equivalence principle, black holes, gravitational waves, and the 1919 eclipse mean general relativity. When the giveaway names both versions, “relativity” or “theory of relativity” is enough.
trap.line: Real answer line: relativity (accept theory of relativity, special relativity, or general relativity; prompt on Einstein’s theory)

topics.name: Simple machines
topics.kicker: Six basic devices that multiply force · Levers, pulleys, ramps, and more
topics.dates: Five listed by Hero of Alexandria, 1st century CE
topics.briefing: Simple machines are the six basic devices that make work easier: the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, and screw. None of them gives you free energy; instead, they trade force for distance, letting you lift a heavy load with a small push over a longer path. The Greek scientist Archimedes studied levers and pulleys and is said to have boasted, “Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth.”
topics.answerHtml: simple machines (accept simple machine; prompt on machines; do not accept a single machine such as “lever” or “pulley”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Hero of Alexandria listed five of these devices in his _Mechanics_, and Renaissance scientists later added a sixth to make the classic set. Archimedes [“ar-kih-MEE-deez”] is said to have boasted about one of them, “Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these basic devices, such as the lever and the pulley, that change the size or direction of a force.

tossups.p: Simon Stevin [“stay-VIN”] explained one of these devices by imagining a loop of beads draped over a triangular block, a picture called the “wreath of spheres.” Another of these devices is just a sloping surface wrapped around a cylinder, and a third is two sloping surfaces placed back to back.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these six devices, which include the screw, the wedge, and the inclined plane.

tossups.p: According to Plutarch, Archimedes used a combination of one kind of these devices to move a fully loaded ship all by himself. A block and tackle, built from several of that same kind of device, has an ideal mechanical advantage equal to the number of rope segments holding up the load.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices, including the lever and the pulley, that make work easier.

tossups.p: The shaduf [“shah-DOOF”], used to lift irrigation water in ancient Egypt, is a pole with a counterweight that acts as one of these devices. That device comes in three classes, depending on whether the fulcrum, the load, or the effort sits in the middle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these basic devices, which also include the wheel and axle and the inclined plane.

tossups.p: The ideal mechanical advantage of one of these devices equals the radius of its wheel divided by the radius of its axle, and for another, it equals the length of a ramp divided by its height. In both cases, that ratio tells how many times the device multiplies the force you apply.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these six devices, such as levers and pulleys, that trade force for distance.

tossups.p: A spiral inside a tube, named for Archimedes, raises water when it is turned, and Archimedes also worked out a law describing how one of these devices balances. Mechanical advantage, the output force divided by the input force, measures how much one of these devices multiplies a force.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these basic devices, including the wedge, the screw, and the lever.

tossups.p: The distance between neighboring threads on one of these devices is called its pitch, and finer threads give that device a greater mechanical advantage. Another of these devices splits wood or holds a door open and is really two ramps placed back to back.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these six devices, which also include the pulley and the lever.

tossups.p: A single fixed version of one of these devices changes only the direction of a force, while a single movable version of it cuts the force needed to lift a load in half. Flagpoles use the fixed version to raise a flag by pulling down on a rope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices, such as the pulley, the lever, and the inclined plane.

tossups.p: Your forearm acts as a third-class version of one of these devices, with the elbow as the pivot and the biceps pulling in between. Seesaws, wheelbarrows, and tweezers are examples of that same device, each of a different class.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these six basic devices, which include the lever and the screw.

tossups.p: A hand-held can opener combines several of these devices, using a turning handle and a sharp cutting wheel. Scissors are two of one kind of these devices joined at a pivot, with blades that act as another kind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these basic devices, such as the lever and the wedge, that make work easier.

tossups.p: The ideal mechanical advantage of any of these devices equals the distance the effort moves divided by the distance the load moves. The efficiency of one of these devices is its useful work output divided by its work input, and friction keeps every real one below 100 percent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these six devices, including the pulley and the wheel and axle.

tossups.p: A windlass, which winds up a rope to raise a bucket from a well, is one of these devices, as are a doorknob and a screwdriver handle. In that device, a large turning part multiplies the force on a smaller rod at its center.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these six basic devices, which include the wheel and axle and the pulley.

tossups.p: The ancient Egyptians are thought to have used long ramps, one of these devices, to drag heavy stone blocks up the pyramids. A longer, gentler ramp needs less force to push a load up, but the load must travel farther.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these six devices, including the inclined plane, the lever, and the screw.

tossups.p: For one of these devices, the ideal mechanical advantage equals the length of the effort arm divided by the length of the load arm, a rule worked out by Archimedes. Moving the pivot of that device closer to the load makes the load easier to lift.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these basic devices, such as the lever, that make work easier.

tossups.p: A zipper’s slider uses small versions of one of these devices to push its teeth together and pry them apart. Axes, knives, and chisels are also examples of that device, which has two sloping sides that meet at a sharp edge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these six devices, including the wedge and the pulley, that change the size or direction of a force.

trap.title: The group, not one
trap.body: These tossups ask for the whole group, so naming one member, like “lever” or “pulley,” is wrong even if the clue you buzzed on was about that one device. Real quiz bowl also writes separate tossups on single machines (the lever, the pulley, the screw, the inclined plane), so the giveaway decides: “these six devices” means the group, while “this device” wants just one. Torque and mechanical advantage are related answers too.
trap.fix: If the question says “these devices” or lists several (lever, pulley, wedge…), say “simple machines.” If it says “this device” with a fulcrum or three classes, say “lever”; a rope over a grooved wheel, “pulley”; a ramp, “inclined plane”; threads and pitch, “screw.” For “output force divided by input force,” say “mechanical advantage.”
